Eggs of the Black-capped bulbul (Rubigula melanictera) are typically incubated within a narrow thermal window, and field data indicate that successful hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 12.5 days at 38 °C [T = 38 °C]; this developmental duration, recorded as the age at birth of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days], is consistent with the relatively short incubation periods found among many small-bodied pycnonotids in tropical lowland forests. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably low initial wet weight of 2.78 grams [Ww0 = 2.78 grams], a mass that corresponds to only a small fraction of the adult body size and necessitates an intense period of parental provisioning. This modest starting mass underscores the high energetic demands of early development, as the chick must more than decuple its weight before fledging. The hatchlings are entirely dependent on both parents for brooding and food delivery, and their rapid growth trajectory is fueled primarily by a diet of soft-bodied insects and fruit pulp provided at frequent intervals throughout the day.

Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic state, typically 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], several key developmental and life-history milestones have been quantified for the Black-capped bulbul in its native dry-zone habitats of Sri Lanka. This body temperature, which represents the normothermic core temperature during routine activity, forms the backdrop against which growth and maturation rates are calibrated. The fledging stage, defined as the time since birth at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight, is typically reached 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period that is characteristic of many tropical passerines facing high nest predation pressure at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This abbreviated developmental phase forces the nestlings to accumulate sufficient feather development and neuromuscular coordination in under two weeks.

Sexual maturity, or the time since birth at puberty, is attained at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] in captive-reared individuals of Rubigula melanictera maintained at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This remarkably early onset of gonadal maturation, occurring just over a month after fledging, stands in contrast to many temperate-zone passerines that delay reproductive maturation until the following breeding season. The rapid sexual development observed in this species is thought to be an adaptation to the aseasonal or weakly seasonal rainfall patterns of its tropical environment, where suitable breeding conditions can arise unpredictably throughout the year. However, despite achieving physiological maturity early, the birds do not immediately breed; instead, they typically defer their first reproductive attempt until they have had sufficient time to establish a territory and secure a mate.

Consequently, the time since birth at first brood, or the age at first successful reproduction, is considerably longer than the age at puberty, occurring at 1.1 years after hatching [tR = 1.1 years after hatching] under the same thermoneutral conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This eleven-month delay between achieving sexual competence and actually initiating a clutch reflects the substantial social and ecological challenges faced by young birds in securing a high-quality breeding territory within a saturated adult population. The annual reproductive output of females is structured around a strategy of multiple nesting attempts per season. Field observations confirm that females produce 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch], a standard clutch size for many Pycnonotidae, and they typically initiate 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year], allowing for either replacement of failed nests or successful double brooding when environmental conditions are favorable.

Maximum longevity in the Black-capped bulbul has been estimated from both ringing returns and captive records, with the oldest documented individuals reaching a maximum lifespan of 11.8 years [am = 11.8 years] when housed under controlled, predator-free conditions at an average ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan is relatively modest compared to some other tropical passerines of equivalent adult size, likely reflecting the metabolic costs associated with its rapid developmental pace and high basal energy demands. Indeed, the resting metabolic rate, measured as the maximum basal oxygen consumption in post-absorptive adults during the inactive phase of their diurnal cycle, was recorded at 52.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 52.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value that aligns with allometric predictions for a bird of this body size. The maximum adult body mass attained by females, recorded as the ultimate wet weight for females, is 29.3 grams [Wwi = 29.3 grams], a figure that represents the upper plateau of the species' mass range and is typically achieved just prior to laying. This combination of a low birth mass, a rapid growth and maturation schedule, multiple annual clutches, and a moderately brief lifespan frames the Black-capped bulbul as a classic example of a fast-paced, tropical life-history strategy optimized for high replacement rates in a relatively stable but predation-prone environment.
